common_name: Mojo Pittosporum (Compact Cold-Hardy Variegated Mock Orange)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mojo was selected in part for improved cold tolerance compared with older tobira variegates, extending its useful range for Gulf Coast gardens that occasionally see hard winter lows.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mojo tolerates coastal salt spray, wind, and poor soil better than many broadleaf evergreens, making it a reliable low hedge or foundation plant in Gulf Coast landscapes. This patented dwarf selection bears small, glossy leaves crisply edged in bright creamy white around a gray-green center, giving a tighter, more compact mound than older variegated tobira cultivars while holding its bright color well in part shade. Clusters of small, cream-white flowers open in spring with the strong orange-blossom fragrance typical of the species. Its dense, naturally tidy habit needs little shearing, and breeders selected it in part for sturdier performance through occasional winter cold snaps at the northern edge of its range.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Nanum keeps a naturally tight, rounded mound and needs far less corrective shearing than the straight species when used as a low hedge or edging plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Nanum tolerates coastal salt spray, wind, and poor soil better than many broadleaf evergreens, and its compact, ball-shaped habit suits it to edging, low hedges, and small border gardens where the full-size species would quickly outgrow its space. Small, leathery, glossy dark-green leaves clothe a dense, slow-growing mound that holds its neat rounded form for years with only light shearing. Clusters of small, creamy-white flowers open at the branch tips in spring, carrying the strong orange-blossom fragrance the species is known for. It is a good choice for small coastal gardens or containers where a Buxus-like formal shape is wanted without the disease issues that can trouble true boxwood in humid climates.

common_name: Golf Ball Kohuhu (Dense Rounded Green Pittosporum)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Golf Ball keeps its dense, naturally spherical shape with little to no pruning, unlike Pittosporum tobira selections that need regular shearing to hold a rounded form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, where leaf color and density are best with a few hours of direct sun. Golf Ball is a naturally globe-shaped selection of kohuhu with small, glossy, bright-green, wavy-edged leaves on fine, near-black stems, forming a dense, symmetrical mound that lives up to its name without any clipping. Small, honey-scented, dark purple flowers appear inconspicuously in late spring, more noticeable by fragrance at dusk than by sight. Its tidy, low-maintenance form and tolerance of coastal wind and salt spray make it a popular low hedge, edging plant, or formal accent, and it withstands shearing well if an even more precise shape is desired.
